allowed_claims: Buttondown includes a WYSIWYG editor in addition to its Markdown editor.
Fancy mode lets users view and edit emails in a format resembling how they will appear when sent.
Fancy mode components can be accessed from the editor toolbar or by typing "/" on a new line.
Fancy mode supports text color, bold, italic, links, left/center/right paragraph alignment, superscript, subscript, and font selection.
Text formatting options appear in a tooltip after the user selects text.
Fancy mode offers the email-safe font options Inter, Comic Sans, cursive, serif, monospace, and default.
Fancy mode fully supports emojis.
Typing a colon followed by an emoji description, such as ":happy", displays emoji suggestions.
A block quote can be added by typing ">" followed by a space.
Text in a pull quote is italicized and centered, unlike a block quote.
Buttondown formats tables with a subtle border by default and lets users remove the border to align items horizontally as a design element.
Poetry blocks preserve text spacing when published and are internally rendered as <pre> tags.
Code blocks are automatically syntax-highlighted based on their programming language.
A code block can be added by typing three backticks followed by the programming language and pressing Enter.
Adding a footnote creates both a reference and a footnote at the bottom of the editor.
Deleting a footnote reference also deletes its corresponding footnote.
A footnote can be added by typing [^text], where "text" is any string sequence.
Fancy mode can write and render LaTeX as blocks, but not inline with text.
A LaTeX block can be added by putting an expression inside two dollar signs and pressing Space or Enter.
Users can switch between Markdown and Fancy mode without losing a LaTeX block.
A divider is a horizontal line between two pieces of content and can be added by typing three dashes or underscores and pressing Space or Enter.
Fancy mode lets users upload their own images.
Buttondown has a built-in Unsplash integration for searching and embedding stock images without leaving the app.
Users can add an Unsplash image by choosing "Find image on Unsplash" from the slash menu, searching in the modal, and selecting an image.
An image can be uploaded by dragging and dropping it into the editor or typing "/image" on a new line and attaching the file.
Uploaded images can have captions that appear below the image for all readers.
Users can turn an image into a link with the "Add link" button beneath the image.
Image alt text can be set by clicking the "Edit" button beneath the image.
Buttondown can generate image alt text, and users can instead write their own or combine both approaches.
Images can be assigned a class name for use with custom CSS.
Buttondown compresses images by default to reduce email size, and users can turn compression off from the image's "Edit" button.
A webwall displays the content below it only on the web and excludes that content from emails sent to email clients.
An emailwall displays the content below it only in subscriber emails and excludes that content from the web version.
A paywall restricts content to premium subscribers.
A subscription wall gates archive content behind a subscription: free and paid subscribers can see the full post, while non-subscribers see only a teaser.
A subscription wall does not require paid subscriptions to be configured.
Fancy mode can add a subscription form that lets readers subscribe to a newsletter from within the email.
A subscription button is a CTA button linking to the newsletter's URL, where people can subscribe.
Free-only blocks display content only to free subscribers, while premium-only blocks display content only to premium subscribers.
Filtered blocks limit only the content inside the block to a selected audience, whereas a wall affects all following content.
Buttondown filtered blocks have five variants: Email only, Web only, Subscribers only, Paid only, and Free only, each with audience-specific visibility.
A filtered block can be added from the slash menu by typing a variant such as "/email" or selecting it from the menu.
Filtered blocks work inside list items and quotes and survive switching to Markdown mode and back.
Fancy mode can link to another email through the normal link interface.
The internal-link interface can be opened from selected text with the toolbar or ⌘K/Ctrl+K, or without selected text through "/link" or ⌘K/Ctrl+K.
The link bar lets users search their emails or select one from a displayed list.
Typing two opening square brackets ("[[") lets users search for and link to another email.
Snippets are reusable content blocks that can be inserted with "/snippet" or the command menu.
Surveys let subscribers answer a question inside an email.
Users can find a survey by code or question through the slash menu, and Buttondown inserts the survey's {{ survey.code }} tag.
Buttondown surveys render in transactional emails, including welcome emails.
Comments add internal notes to an email that subscribers cannot see and that can be used personally or shared with a team.
Buttondown does not support native audio uploads and states that it has no active plans to add them.
Buttondown has integrations with SoundCloud, YouTube, Transistor, Spotify, and Vimeo for externally hosted audio.
Buttondown does not host video.
Dropping a video file into the editor attaches it as a downloadable file instead of embedding an inline player.
Pasting the URL of a hosted video into an email causes Buttondown to automatically embed a player.
Buttondown integrates with YouTube and Vimeo for playable video embeds.
Buttondown lets users add file attachments to emails.
Buttondown attachment formats include PDF, DOC, DOCX, TXT, MD, JPG, JPEG, PNG, GIF, WEBP, ZIP, MP3, MP4, CSV, EPUB, and ICS.
For files larger than 1 MiB, Buttondown recommends uploading them to a service such as Dropbox, Google Drive, or AWS S3 and linking to them in the email.
In Fancy mode, users add an attachment by typing "/attachments" and selecting a file; in Markdown mode, they drag and drop the file into the editor.
When an email with attachments is sent, Buttondown automatically includes those attachments in the outgoing emails.
Recipients see Buttondown email attachments according to their email client's display conventions.
Attachments are available to download from Buttondown web archive views.
Adding attachments to emails is a premium Buttondown feature; free accounts must upgrade to a paid plan to use it.
Buttondown supports composing newsletters in Markdown.
Buttondown’s editor supports both WYSIWYG rich-text editing and Markdown.
Buttondown automatically renders text surrounded by double asterisks as bold.
The Buttondown CLI lets users manage newsletter content from a local machine.
The Buttondown CLI supports editing newsletters in a preferred text editor.
The Buttondown CLI supports workflows for backing up newsletter content.
The Buttondown CLI supports syncing media files.
The Buttondown CLI supports working offline with newsletter content.
The Buttondown CLI lets users edit newsletters as Markdown in their preferred editor.
Newsletter files managed through the Buttondown CLI can be version-controlled with Git or other version-control tools.
The Buttondown CLI can sync newsletter content bidirectionally between a computer and Buttondown.
The Buttondown CLI can manage media files such as images and attachments.
The Buttondown CLI supports workflow automation with scripts.
The Buttondown CLI can be installed globally through npm as `@buttondown/cli`.
The Buttondown CLI can be run with npx without installing it globally.
`buttondown login` authenticates the CLI using a Buttondown API key found in Buttondown settings.
`buttondown pull` downloads newsletters from Buttondown and creates a local `./buttondown` directory containing the content.
`buttondown create --title="My Newsletter Issue #1"` creates a new local draft whose Markdown file can be edited in a preferred editor.
`buttondown push` saves local changes back to Buttondown.
`buttondown push` does not publish emails whose frontmatter has `status: draft`, which is the default status for newly created emails.
When `buttondown push` runs, it synchronizes content while preserving the status specified in each email’s frontmatter.
An email with `status: draft` remains a draft when pushed through the Buttondown CLI.
An email with `status: scheduled` will be sent at its specified `publish_date`.
An email with `status: about_to_send` is queued and will typically be sent within a few minutes.
Editing and pushing an email with `status: sent` changes its body in the archives.
The Buttondown CLI creates a project structure containing `.buttondown.json`, an `emails/` directory for Markdown newsletter content, and a `media/` directory for images and attachments.
The Buttondown CLI stores each newsletter as a Markdown file with YAML frontmatter.
For API email creation, `subject` is the only field that is always required.
The `buttondown create` command requires a string `title`, which becomes the email subject.
Buttondown email bodies accept HTML or Markdown and default to an empty string when omitted.
The documented default value of the Buttondown email `status` field is `about_to_send`.
The documented default value of the Buttondown email `email_type` field is `public`.
Buttondown supports an optional `slug` field with a default value of `null`.
Buttondown supports an optional human-readable `description` field that defaults to an empty string.
Buttondown supports an optional primary-image URL field named `image` that defaults to an empty string.
Buttondown supports an optional datetime `publish_date` field that defaults to `null`.
Buttondown’s optional `attachments` field accepts an array of attachment UUIDs and defaults to an empty array.
Buttondown supports an optional object-valued `metadata` field for custom metadata, defaulting to an empty object.
Buttondown supports an optional `canonical_url` string for the original content URL, defaulting to an empty string.
Buttondown supports an optional integer `secondary_id` as an informal issue number, defaulting to `null`.
Buttondown supports object-valued subscriber filtering rules through the optional `filters` field, which defaults to `FilterGroup()`.
Buttondown supports an optional `commenting_mode` string for comment settings, defaulting to `enabled`.
Buttondown supports an optional `related_email_ids` array for related email IDs, defaulting to an empty array.
Buttondown supports an optional boolean `featured` field for archive highlighting, defaulting to `false`.
Buttondown supports six documented email visibility types: `public`, `private`, `premium`, `free`, `churned`, and `archival`.
Buttondown supports the documented email statuses `draft`, `about_to_send`, `scheduled`, `in_flight`, `sent`, `paused`, and `imported`.
Buttondown email subject lines have a maximum length of 1000 characters.
Buttondown validates email subject lines against XSS attacks.
A Buttondown email subject cannot be empty when the email is created through the API.
Buttondown email body content can be HTML or Markdown.
Buttondown does not allow null characters in email body content.
Buttondown validates email body content against XSS attacks.
Buttondown defaults an omitted email body to an empty string.
Buttondown email slugs must be URL-safe and are validated with Django’s `validate_slug`.
Buttondown email slugs have a maximum length of 100 characters.
A Buttondown email slug must be unique within the newsletter.
Buttondown automatically generates an email slug from the subject when no slug is provided.
When local images are placed in the CLI project’s `media/` directory and referenced from Markdown, `buttondown push` uploads them and updates their URLs.
The Buttondown CLI can work with multiple newsletters by pulling each one into a different directory using `--directory`.
Buttondown CLI newsletter content can be managed in a Git repository by initializing Git, pulling content, and committing the files.
`buttondown logout` clears stored Buttondown CLI credentials.

When the same email is modified both locally and in Buttondown, the documented conflict workflow is to back up local changes, run `buttondown pull --force`, manually merge differences, and push the resolution.
The Buttondown CLI reports `Error: --title is required for the create command` when a create command is missing its title.
The Buttondown CLI reports `Skipping [file]: Invalid format (missing frontmatter)` for a file missing required frontmatter.
For image upload failures, the Buttondown CLI reports `Failed to upload image [filename]: [error message]`.
For API errors, the Buttondown CLI reports `Failed to create email: [error details]`.
Buttondown provides support for CLI questions at support@buttondown.com.
Buttondown automations can build custom sequences for new subscribers.
Buttondown automations can create flows for tagged subscribers.
Buttondown automations can survey customers to personalize their content.
Buttondown automations let publishers control when and how each email is sent.
By default, Buttondown does not collect data about publishers or their subscribers.
Buttondown's subscriber-behavior and email-performance analytics can be enabled in one click.
Buttondown's editor supports native Markdown.
Buttondown can publish a mailing list as an RSS feed.
Buttondown can turn an existing blog's RSS feed into a mailing list published at a chosen frequency.
Buttondown provides a REST API with webhooks and documentation.
Buttondown states that anything users can do in its app can also be done through its REST API.
Buttondown lets publishers enable or disable comments on posts.
Buttondown includes a comments interface where readers can talk with one another and stay connected with the publisher.
Comments are a first-party Buttondown feature that can be used in automations and integrations.
Buttondown surveys can gather feedback, conduct polls, and collect insights for tailoring newsletter content.
Subscribers answer Buttondown surveys in their browser.
Buttondown delivers survey results to the publisher's inbox and analytics pages.
Buttondown survey respondents do not have to click through to a third-party site.
Buttondown states that survey respondents' data is not sold to advertisers.
Buttondown sponsorships let sponsors browse available slots, pay through Stripe, and submit their own content.
Publishers approve sponsor content before it is sent through Buttondown.
Buttondown newsletters can include file, document, and other content attachments.
Buttondown supports over 40 integrations for embedding videos, GIFs, songs, posts, and other content.
Buttondown lets publishers send a newsletter directly from a personal or business email client.
A publisher can send an email to Buttondown from the address used to join Buttondown and have it sent to subscribers.
A publisher can email Buttondown to save a newsletter as a draft instead of sending it.
Buttondown's CLI can draft, schedule, and analyze emails from a terminal.
Buttondown's CLI supports writing in Vim, VS Code, or another editor.
Buttondown's CLI can keep newsletter drafts in Git alongside code and sync them to Buttondown.
Buttondown's CLI can script newsletters from CI/CD pipelines.
Buttondown's CLI can bulk-manage subscribers.
Buttondown's CLI can pull analytics.
Buttondown states that anything users can do in its web app can also be done from its CLI.
Buttondown lets an account create an unlimited number of distinct newsletters.
Buttondown can publish newsletters to the web as shareable archives.
Buttondown archives provide permalinks and let people browse a newsletter's past issues.
Buttondown lets publishers hide specific emails from their archives.
Buttondown lets publishers turn off public archives and use email only.
Buttondown allows unlimited contributor accounts for managing newsletters.
Buttondown lets publishers set specific permissions for each contributor.
Buttondown's Teams tool is available on the Professional plan.
Buttondown's Teams tool lets multiple people manage a newsletter.
Buttondown places no limit on the number of teammates collaborating on a newsletter.
Creating a Buttondown team requires a paid Buttondown account.
Creating a Buttondown team requires a newsletter username, email address, author name, and description.
Buttondown lets team owners invite teammates and configure what they are permitted to access and do.
After a teammate is invited, Buttondown emails the invitation and shows that teammate as Pending in the Teams menu.
A Buttondown team invitation contains a link the invitee can use to accept and collaborate on the newsletter.
Invitees who already have Buttondown accounts are directed to sign in when accepting a team invitation.
Buttondown automatically creates a free account for a team invitee who does not already have an account.
After a teammate accepts a Buttondown invitation, they can begin working on the newsletter and their status changes from Pending to Accepted.
A Buttondown newsletter's Author name remains the same regardless of how many teammates collaborate on it.
A Buttondown newsletter's Author name can be changed in Email settings.
Buttondown permissions control both which parts of a newsletter each teammate can access and what they can do within those parts.
Buttondown's subscriber-management permission can grant access to view, create, and delete subscribers and to view subscriber analytics.
Buttondown's email-management permission can grant access to view and edit emails and to view email reporting and analytics.
Buttondown has a teammate permission specifically for sending emails to subscribers.
Buttondown's Styling & CSS permission can grant access to view or set CSS, frontmatter, and other metadata for a newsletter or its online archives.
Buttondown's Automations permission can grant access to view and create automations for a newsletter.
Buttondown's Surveys permission can grant access to view and create surveys for a newsletter.
Buttondown's Administrivia permission covers settings, domain registration, billing information, lifecycle emails, and administrative areas not covered by the other permission categories.
Except for Sending emails, each Buttondown teammate permission area can be configured as None, Read, or Read & write.
Buttondown lets team owners change a teammate's permissions at any time.
Buttondown lets team owners revoke a teammate's newsletter access, with the permissions updating immediately.
Buttondown lets a user switch between newsletters by selecting the newsletter name in the upper-left corner and choosing another newsletter.
Buttondown provides a REST API for newsletter operations.
Buttondown’s API can manage subscribers.
Buttondown’s API can send emails.
Buttondown’s API can create automations.
Applications can use Buttondown’s API to handle paid subscriptions.
Buttondown can connect to analytics systems through its API.
Buttondown can connect to a CRM through its API.
Buttondown can connect to internal tools through its API.
Buttondown’s API can synchronize subscriber data.
Buttondown can trigger emails from external events.
Developers can build their own dashboard using Buttondown’s API.
Every Buttondown feature is built API-first, and Buttondown uses the same API to power its own app.
Buttondown states that anything available through its interface can be scripted through its API.
The Buttondown API is available on every plan, including the free plan.
Buttondown’s API is rate-limited to prevent abuse.
Buttondown API keys are available from the API keys page in a Buttondown account.
Buttondown users can create multiple API keys with different permissions.
Buttondown does not provide an official SDK for any programming language.
Buttondown maintains an OpenAPI specification intended to serve callers regardless of language or framework.
Buttondown does not provide an official MCP server.
Buttondown customer support is provided by a team of real humans rather than chatbots.
Buttondown’s distributed support team is generally available from 6am–6pm US Eastern time, excluding weekends and major holidays.
Buttondown support handles feature questions, email deliverability questions, and account-management help.
Buttondown offers migration help to people moving their newsletters from another platform.
Buttondown offers automations, personalizations, and an editor for targeting messages.
Buttondown describes its API as feature-complete.
Buttondown provides personalization and automation features.
Buttondown provides analytics intended to show users what is working and how.
Buttondown supports inviting an entire team and collaborating on larger initiatives.
Buttondown can connect email workflows to Discord.
Buttondown can connect email workflows to Memberful.
Buttondown can connect email workflows to YouTube.
Buttondown lets users skip logging in and post directly from their own email.
Buttondown can cross-post content from other platforms to a mailing list.
Buttondown offers one-click concierge migration for an entire mailing list, regardless of its size.
Buttondown collaborators can review email drafts before they are sent, see drafts, and suggest changes.
Buttondown lets newsletter owners control what each collaborator can see and do.
Buttondown can give an editor access to drafts without giving them access to billing.
Buttondown can let a marketing lead manage subscribers without access to API keys.
Buttondown collaborators can be invited by email.
Buttondown supports multiple collaborator roles, ranging from read-only reviewers to full admins.
Buttondown provides an audit trail showing who did what and when across a newsletter.
Buttondown collaborator roles can grant full sending permissions or restrict collaborators to drafting only.
Buttondown does not limit how many collaborators can be invited.
Buttondown email attachments should be no larger than 2 MB.
A Buttondown email can have up to 3 attached files.
Buttondown offers a demo site for hands-on feature exploration.
Buttondown is browser-based and requires no installation.

Creating a Buttondown account requires a browser with cookies, JavaScript, and in-browser pop-ups enabled, an active email address whose password the registrant knows, and a strong Buttondown password.
A Buttondown username forms part of the user's public Buttondown URL and can be changed later.
Buttondown uses the account email address for notifications, account updates, and billing information.
When sending through Buttondown's server, subscribers do not see the account's registered email address.
Newsletters sent from the Buttondown server use a subscriber-visible sender address formatted as username@buttondown.email.
Buttondown supports sending a newsletter from a custom domain.
After account creation, Buttondown sends a confirmation email from justin@buttondown.email containing an account-verification link.
Buttondown newsletter branding can include a name, description, colors, and logo.
Buttondown supports sharing a newsletter URL, embedding subscription forms, and importing existing subscribers to build a subscriber base.
Buttondown supports customizing email appearance with templates and CSS.
Buttondown supports drafting, previewing, and sending a newsletter.
Buttondown provides migration guides for users coming from another newsletter platform.
Buttondown provides an API reference and a CLI guide for programmers.
Buttondown offers setup help through concierge@buttondown.com.
Buttondown accepts bug reports, feature requests, and general feedback through GitHub Discussions.
Buttondown provides a customer-support contact channel.

assets.content:
Subject: Editing and sending are separate permissions
Preview text: Grant access to create and edit emails while keeping subscriber sends under separate control.

Hi there,

A writer and editor can work on the same newsletter without sharing one broad role.

Buttondown is email newsletter software with configurable teammate permissions. An owner can grant Read & write access to email management—which covers viewing, editing, and creating emails—while withholding the separate permission to send emails to subscribers.

Other permission areas can be configured as None, Read, or Read & write. Sending is handled separately, so the person editing an issue does not automatically need authority to send it.

Teams is available on the Professional plan. The official Teams documentation lists the permission areas and their configurations, letting you check the available boundaries against the writing, editing, and sending split you need.

See the Teams permission list → https://docs.buttondown.com/teams

- Buttondown

brief.promise: Buttondown is worth evaluating when a newsletter owner needs a writer and editor to collaborate without automatically giving every teammate the same authority.
brief.orientation: Buttondown is newsletter software for an owner and teammates who need to divide drafting, management, sending, and administrative access within one publishing workflow.
brief.arc: In this single email, move from the familiar writer-and-editor handoff to Buttondown's specific permission mechanism, disclose that Teams requires a paid account, and offer the documentation as a proportionate way to judge fit before registering.
brief.sequence_rationale: A solution-aware reader does not need a long explanation of collaborative publishing. One email can lead with the relevant division of responsibility, make the mechanism concrete, answer the broad-access concern, and send the reader to the official Teams documentation. No urgency, prior interaction, completed migration, or recipient-specific workflow is assumed.

emails.selection_reason: Configurable teammate access and a separate sending permission directly address the qualified writer-plus-editor workflow and give the reader a concrete, checkable reason to evaluate Buttondown.
emails.target_audience: A newsletter owner bringing an editor or operations teammate into a formerly solo publishing workflow
emails.job: Earn an informed evaluation of whether Buttondown's documented teammate permissions suit the reader's desired division between editing and sending.
emails.single_idea: Buttondown lets a newsletter owner invite teammates, configure what they may access and do, and control sending through a distinct permission, so a writer-and-editor team can evaluate a shared workflow without assuming everyone needs equivalent authority.
emails.felt_need: A second operator wanted permissions that could be granted or revoked independently because fixed, tiered roles did not accommodate their edge case. For one publication lead, handling the newsletter operation alone for six months was experienced as excessive, motivating a divided team workflow.
emails.mechanism: In Buttondown Teams, the owner invites teammates and configures their access; sending emails is its own permission. Creating a team requires a paid Buttondown account. The official Teams documentation lets the reader inspect these boundaries before deciding whether to evaluate the product further.
emails.belief_shift: Before: evaluating a shared newsletter tool may seem to require accepting one broad collaborator role. After: Buttondown documents configurable teammate access and a distinct sending permission that can be checked against the team's writer-and-editor boundary.
must_not_say: Do not claim Buttondown offers an arbitrary action-level or mix-and-match permission checklist for every edge case.
Do not promise reduced workload, faster publishing, fewer errors, or a better editorial outcome.
Do not state or imply that the recipient currently uses Google Docs, shares credentials, has suffered a permissions failure, or uses any named newsletter platform.
Do not claim Teams is free; creating a Buttondown team requires a paid account.
Do not generalize established fit beyond the qualified writer-plus-editor slice.
Do not claim competitors lack equivalent permissions or that Buttondown is unique.
Do not add testimonials, adoption claims, invented urgency, migration claims, API security claims, or unrelated editor features.

emails.objection: Would an editor need the same control as the newsletter owner? Buttondown documents configurable teammate access and treats sending as a distinct permission, though the reader still needs to check whether the available boundaries match their exact workflow.
emails.tone: Matter-of-fact, concise, and candid about the paid-account prerequisite.
emails.call_to_action: Review Buttondown's Teams permissions and compare them with the boundary you want between writing, editing, and sending.
emails.next_step_decision: Decide whether Buttondown's documented teammate and sending permissions are close enough to the intended writer-and-editor workflow to justify a fuller product evaluation.
emails.next_step_value: The official Teams documentation shows that owners can invite teammates, configure what they may access and do, and assign a distinct permission for sending emails; it also states that creating a team requires a paid account.
emails.next_step_limit: Reading the documentation does not prove that the available permission granularity covers every edge case, nor does it test the workflow hands-on or establish pricing beyond the paid-account requirement.
emails.subject_strategy: Name the practical writer-versus-sender boundary in plain language; avoid generic collaboration claims, fear-based security framing, competitor references, and urgency.

brief.voice_notes: Use Buttondown's plainspoken, product-confident register. Lead with the practical permission boundary, explain it concretely, and keep any playfulness restrained because this is a first-contact acquisition email.
